The proposal could cost roughly $1.2 trillion, with Trump allies pointing to tariff revenue as one potential funding source.

When asked about supporting the plan against its $1.2 trillion cost amid the growing national debt, Marshall declined to commit. “I’m going to bring in all the information, and then make a decision,” he said, adding he’s disagreed with Trump before “and it probably won’t be the last.”
Marshall added, “Instead, I said, I’m going to be focused on Kansas jobs. I’m going to be focused on protecting Kansas agriculture and the Kansas cattle industry.”
Marshall Takes More Cautious Stance

The comments marked a more cautious stance than Marshall’s Wednesday post on X, where Marshall wrote, “Comment how you will spend your $5,000 Trump Dividend when Republicans win in November,” signaling his support for the plan.
Comment how you will spend your $5,000 Trump Dividend when Republicans win in November.
Marshall, who has Trump’s endorsement, has also voiced dissent about Trump administration policy when the president threatened to ban
Bombardier
, the Canadian jet maker, from selling planes in the U.S. as part of the ongoing trade war with Canada.
“I’m going to fight to keep Bombardier’s over 1,200 Kansas jobs. I’ve already taken that concern inside the Oval Office,” Marshall posted on X.

Hamilton’s Long Odds in Kansas
Hamilton faces an uphill climb to win in November. A Democrat has not won a Senate race in the Sunflower State since 1932, although the state’s two-term governor, Laura Kelly, is a Democrat.

Hamilton’s campaign did receive a glimmer of hope in August when election handicapper Sabato’s Crystal Ball shifted the Kansas Senate race from safe Republican to likely Republican following Hamilton’s Democratic primary win.
The current remarks from Marshall indicate he is balancing loyalty to Trump with reelection pressures in a state where he holds a comfortable political advantage.
